citation: Hopman AJG, Baart JA, Brand HS. Articaine and neurotoxicity – a review. Br Dent J 2017;223(7):501-506 (read as the Advance Online Publication of 3 October 2017, PDF pages 1-6)
text_quality: ok — PDF text layer, 6 pages (advance-online pagination, not the print issue's 501-506); reading order checked against renders of PDF pages 1 and 5; Table 1 (PDF page 3) read from the layout view; Fig. 1 (PRISMA flow, PDF page 2) is extractable text.
design: Literature review with a systematic search: PubMed and Web of Science with a stated query (paraesthesia/neurotoxicity terms AND articaine brand names), reference lists hand-searched, PRISMA flow diagram; inclusion: retrospective studies and clinical trials reporting an incidence of paraesthesia or its frequency relative to market share, and animal or in vitro studies only if articaine was compared with other anaesthetics; one author screened titles, two read the 47 full texts; qualitative synthesis only (no meta-analysis, no risk-of-bias assessment, search dates not stated). Internal count inconsistency: Fig. 1 gives 16 studies included in qualitative synthesis (4 in vitro/animal), the text gives 16 clinical plus four in vitro studies, and the laboratory section discusses five studies (refs 26-30: two rat, three cell culture). The review does not cite or discuss Hillerup, Bakke, Larsen, Thomsen & Gerds 2011 (the rat sciatic-nerve electrophysiology/stereology study, PMID 21467556); its only Hillerup reference is Hillerup, Jensen & Ersbøll 2011 (J Am Dent Assoc, Danish Medicines Agency registry plus clinical sample, PMID 21531935), cited in Table 1 (PDF page 3), on PDF page 4 and on PDF page 5 ('This suggestion is rejected by Hillerup and colleagues', the suggestion being that inexperienced dentists' needle trauma explains articaine's over-representation).
population: Published studies of paraesthesia after dental local anaesthesia: Ontario professional-liability reports (Haas & Lennon 1995, 1996; Gaffen & Haas 2009), US FDA adverse-event reports (Garisto 2010; Piccinni 2015), Danish insurance and Danish Medicines Agency data (Legarth 2005; Hillerup, Jensen & Ersbøll 2011), German manufacturer reports (Rahn 2000), a Dutch dentist questionnaire (NMT 2004), UK Yellow Card reports (Zahedi 2012), UCSF oral-surgery referral series (Pogrel 2007, 2012), one set of prospective randomised trials (Malamed 2001); two rat studies (Ribeiro 2003, Baroni 2013) and three cell-culture studies (Werdehausen 2009, 2012; Malet 2015).
n: 128 records screened, 47 full texts assessed, 31 excluded; Fig. 1: 16 studies in the qualitative synthesis (4 in vitro/animal); text: 16 clinical and four in vitro studies; 34 references. Malamed 2001 as described: 1,325 people followed up by telephone.
setting: Dentistry (mostly mandibular/inferior alveolar nerve blocks); data from Canada, USA, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands and the UK, 1973-2011; authors at the Academic Centre for Dentistry Amsterdam (ACTA) and VU Medical Centre.
intervention: Articaine with adrenaline as sold in dental cartridges (at its marketed concentration, which the review notes is higher than that of most other dental anaesthetics).
comparator: Other dental local anaesthetics (lidocaine, prilocaine at two marketed strengths, mepivacaine, bupivacaine) and, in the registry studies, each drug's market share; in the cell studies also tetracaine, ropivacaine and procaine; saline/adrenaline-only arms in the rat studies.
route: Clinical: dental injection, mostly mandibular block, some infiltration. Animal: subcutaneous implantation of anaesthetic-soaked paper cones (Ribeiro 2003); injection near the mental nerve region of the rat jaw (Baroni 2013). In vitro: direct exposure of neuroblastoma or T-lymphoma cells.
duration: Not applicable (review). Persistent paraesthesia defined as lasting at least three months; laboratory exposures 20 minutes to 24 hours; rat follow-up 24 hours (Baroni) and up to 10 days (Ribeiro, per its abstract).
outcomes: Incidence of (persistent) paraesthesia per injection and its share relative to market share; reporting odds ratios; tissue inflammatory reaction in rats; cell death/cytotoxicity in culture.

key_results.quote: In most studies the number of paraesthesia cases after the use of articaine was higher than the market share of this anaesthetic.
In animal studies and in cell culture experiments, however, articaine did not have a higher toxicity compared to other amide anaesthetics.
Ultimately, 16 clinical studies and four in vitro studies were included in this review.
A test group of 1,325 people, who had had articaine or lidocaine injected during dental treatment, were contacted at a later date by phone.
The duration of paraesthesia ranged from less than a day to 18 days after dental treatment.
The market share of the local anaesthetics during the last year of the studied period was examined by the use of a questionnaire. Fourteen cases of paraesthesia were reported in 1993.
No overrepresentation of paraesthesia after use of articaine was observed
Articaine showed the highest reporting odds ratio, suggesting an increased chance of paraesthesia after use.
Articaine induced a higher inflammatory reaction than lidocaine but was comparable with the other anaesthetics investigated.
The cell death was dependent on the concentration of the anaesthetic.
articaine proved to be less toxic than the other evaluated anaesthetics: tetracaine, bupivacaine, prilocaine, mepivacaine, ropivacaine and lidocaine.
in which neuroblastoma cells were exposed to anaesthetics for only 20 minutes … Articaine and ropivacaine proved to be the least toxic
The inflammatory response in the rats injected with articaine did not differ from the group that received a lidocaine injection.
In most retrospective investigations of paraesthesia cases, an overrepresentation of articaine has been reported relative to its market share.
A possible explanation is that articaine is used at a [dose figure omitted]-concentration, a higher concentration than most other anaesthetics.
However, animal and in vitro investigations do not support this suggestion. In most of these studies, articaine was less cytotoxic than, or comparable to, other anaesthetics.
This suggestion is rejected by Hillerup and colleagues.21 In their investigation, 11 patients had damage to two branches of the trigeminal nerve.
Persistent sensibility disorders after administration of local anaesthetics are rare.
However, this observation is not supported by in vitro studies and animal experiments. Further investigation of possible causes of paraesthesia after use of local anaesthetics seems to be warranted.

author_limitations.quote: Retrospective studies are useful to identify rare complications of medication, but are also liable to bias.
The information provided is often incomplete.
This market share is sometimes estimated.

It is also worth noticing that the studies reporting a highly increased risk for paraesthesia after use of articaine, were both based on sales data from the same company, reporting a very small market share for this anaesthetic.
This difference suggests that the search query used during the analysis of a database may have a considerable effect on the outcome.
Media and internet attention for articaine could also lead to an increased awareness and reportage of complaints related to this anaesthetic.
However, the authors did not seem to realise articaine’s lower risk of systemic toxicity.

funding_conflicts: No funding statement and no conflict-of-interest statement appear anywhere in the PDF (checked by text search and on the rendered pages); the only acknowledgement is for linguistic correction. Two authors (Baart, Brand) wrote the textbook cited as reference 1. Checks against abstracts: Hopman describes Lambert 1994 as 'Direct injection', but that study exposed desheathed frog nerves in vitro; it attributes the 64 Ontario cases to 1999-2008 where Gaffen & Haas report 182 reports for 1999-2008 and 64 for 2006-2008; it says articaine's inflammatory response in Baroni 2013 did not differ from lidocaine's, whereas Baroni's abstract grades it moderate against light; it reads Ribeiro 2003 as articaine above lidocaine and comparable to the rest, whereas Ribeiro's abstract places articaine and mepivacaine below bupivacaine.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Hillerup S, Jensen RH, Ersbøll BK. Trigeminal nerve injury associated with injection of local anaesthetics: needle lesion or neurotoxicity? J Am Dent Assoc 2011;142:531-9 (ref 21)
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Hopman's only Hillerup reference (Danish Medicines Agency registry 1995-2007 sales, 292 adverse-reaction reports, clinical sample of 115). Not the rat sciatic-nerve study (PMID 21467556), which Hopman does not cite — decides the C050 question. Probably the 'Hillerup 2011' of Ropivacaine Wheals 6.8a and the 'Danish registry study' of the Reference §4.9.3.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Three randomised double-blind trials, 1,325 subjects, telephone follow-up; paraesthesia lasted under a day to 18 days. Prospective defined-population study — C056.
